analysis.headline: Reported favorably out of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on December 19, 2024 and placed on the Senate Calendar (No. 729), but never received a Senate floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The ETHICS Act would ban Members of Congress, and their spouses and dependent children, from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and similar investments while in office, requiring them to divest such holdings or place them in qualifying blind trusts. Violations would trigger civil penalties, including fines of at least a month's salary or 10% of the value of the non-divested holdings. The bill would also fine officials $500 for failing to file required transaction reports and force financial disclosures to be filed electronically in searchable, downloadable public databases.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who rely on the integrity of lawmaking: the bill would reduce the ability of lawmakers to trade on nonpublic information they encounter in their work, and give the public easier access to disclosure records [S2]. Members' constituents would also gain from published certifications, trust agreements, and penalty records on ethics office websites [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children would be barred from purchasing or selling individual stocks and related instruments that are not diversified funds, Treasury securities, or other specified holdings [S2].
Existing holdings would have to be divested or placed in a qualified blind trust within 120 days of the effective date, with the option to divest within 90 days of enactment for current members [S3].

Violations would carry civil penalties equal to the greater of a month's pay or 10% of the value of each non-divested investment, imposed every 30 days of continuing noncompliance, and the Attorney General could seek fines of $10,000 per communication or 1% of a blind trust's value for leaking trust contents [S3].

Financial disclosure reports and transaction reports of Members and candidates would have to be available online in searchable, sortable, downloadable form with API access, replacing the current harder-to-use records [S3].

The reported substitute expanded coverage to the President and Vice President and added digital assets as covered investments, and barred new qualified blind trusts going forward rather than allowing them as an indefinite shelter [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress themselves — and the wealthiest of them in particular — would bear the direct cost: they would have to sell individual stocks, commodities, futures, and certain other holdings or place them in blind trusts, and would face fines of at least a month's salary or 10% of non-divested value for noncompliance [S3]. Wealthy officeholders with large portfolios, and spouses whose finances were previously untouched by the existing STOCK Act regime, would bear the largest compliance burden.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves significant carve-outs: a spouse's compensation and securities from their primary occupation and corporate board service are excluded, spouses may trade in the course of their own occupation, and investment-grade corporate bonds held at enactment may be kept [S3], so family finances could still be affected by a spouse's career and board seats.

Enforcement depends on the House and Senate ethics offices imposing fines, not on automatic penalties, and the bill's fines for failing to file transaction reports ($500) and the main divestiture regime were set to take effect only on March 31, 2027 in the reported version, delaying real impact for years [S3].

A good-faith objection to stock-trading bans generally is that forcing divestiture or blind trusts imposes real costs and complexity on members and their families, and may discourage qualified people with financial or business backgrounds from serving; the bill's own structure — allowing small holdings under $10,000 for dependent children and phased deadlines with extensions — acknowledges this compliance burden [S3].

Members would also be restricted from controlling or dissolving blind trusts for 90 days after leaving office, and trustees' communications with members would be tightly limited and subject to penalties, which critics could argue is a heavy intrusion into personal financial management [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — closing a loophole that lets lawmakers trade securities while writing the laws and overseeing the industries those companies operate in — is real and widely supported among the bill's 23 cosponsors, and the compliance costs fall on a small, well-resourced group of officeholders rather than the public. The honest counterweights are the carve-outs for spouses' own careers and board service, reliance on ethics offices for enforcement, and a delayed 2027 effective date that would soften and postpone the impact. On balance the bill is a straightforward conflict-of-interest restriction whose main costs are borne by the officials it regulates.

outcome.mechanism: Reported favorably by the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on December 19, 2024 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 729), but never scheduled for a Senate floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 17, 2023 by Sen. Merkley with 23 cosponsors (21 Democrats, 2 Independents) and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S1][S4][S5].
On July 24, 2024, the committee ordered the bill to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably [S5].

On December 19, 2024, the committee reported the bill with an amendment in the nature of a substitute (Report No. 118-309), and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 729 [S5][S3].

The reported substitute expanded the ban to the President and Vice President, added digital assets to covered investments, eliminated new qualified blind trusts as a shelter, and set the main requirements to take effect March 31, 2027 [S3].
No Senate floor vote was taken on the bill, and no companion action is recorded in the House, before the 118th Congress ended [S5][S1].

key_actors.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1171 on April 17, 2023, originally with 24 Democratic and Independent cosponsors listed at introduction, and pursued it through the committee process [S1][S3].

key_actors.name: Sen. Gary Peters
key_actors.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
key_actors.what_they_did: Brought the bill through his committee: ordered it reported favorably on July 24, 2024, and reported it with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on December 19, 2024 (Report No. 118-309) [S5].

key_actors.name: Senate Leadership / Senate floor schedulers
key_actors.what_they_did: Never scheduled S. 1171 for a floor vote after it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on December 19, 2024; the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress without a floor vote [S5].
